questions.q: A metal block measures 0.20 m by 0.10 m by 0.050 m and has a mass of 2.7 kg. What is its density?
A spring obeys Hooke's law and extends by 0.040 m when a force of 6.0 N is applied. What force is needed to extend it by 0.10 m?
questions.solution: Spring constant: \(k = \frac{F}{x} = \frac{6.0}{0.040} = 150\ \text{N m}^{-1}\). Then \(F = kx\) = 150 × 0.10 = 15 N. The value 150 is the spring constant, not the force.

questions.q: A force of 8.0 N stretches a spring by 0.050 m, within its limit of proportionality, as the graph shows. How much elastic strain energy is stored in the spring?

figure.alt: Force against extension: a straight line from the origin to 8.0 newtons at an extension of 0.050 metres. The triangular area under the line is shaded.

questions.solution: The force rises steadily from zero, so the energy is the area of a triangle under the force–extension graph: \(E = \frac{1}{2}F\Delta L\) = 0.5 × 8.0 × 0.050 = 0.20 J. Forgetting the half (0.40 J) is the usual slip.

questions.q: A wire of cross-sectional area \(2.0 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{2}\) supports a load of 50 N. What is the tensile stress in the wire?
questions.solution: Tensile stress is force per unit cross-sectional area: \(\sigma = \frac{F}{A} = \frac{50}{2.0 \times 10^{-7}} = 2.5 \times 10^{8}\ \text{Pa}\).

questions.q: A wire of original length 2.0 m extends by 1.0 mm under load. What is the tensile strain?
questions.solution: Strain is extension divided by original length, with both in the same unit: \(\frac{1.0 \times 10^{-3}}{2.0} = 5.0 \times 10^{-4}\). It is a ratio, so it has no unit.

questions.q: A wire is under a tensile stress of \(2.5 \times 10^{8}\ \text{Pa}\) and has a tensile strain of \(1.25 \times 10^{-3}\). What is the Young modulus of its material?
questions.solution: Young modulus is stress divided by strain: \(E = \frac{2.5 \times 10^{8}}{1.25 \times 10^{-3}} = 2.0 \times 10^{11}\ \text{Pa}\). This is a typical value for steel.

questions.q: The graph shows stress against strain for a metal wire, within its limit of proportionality. What is the Young modulus of the metal?

figure.alt: Stress against strain: a straight line from the origin to a stress of 1.2 times ten to the eight pascals at a strain of 1.0 times ten to the minus three.

questions.solution: The Young modulus is the gradient of the straight-line part of a stress–strain graph. Reading the axes with their powers of ten: \(E = \frac{1.2 \times 10^{8}}{1.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 1.2 \times 10^{11}\ \text{Pa}\).

questions.q: What does the area under a force–extension graph represent?

options.B: The Young modulus of the material.
options.C: The work done in stretching the sample.
options.D: The breaking stress of the material.

questions.solution: Work done is force multiplied by distance moved, so the area under a force–extension graph is the work done in stretching. If the sample is still elastic, this is the elastic strain energy stored.

questions.q: The graph shows stress–strain curves for three materials, X, Y and Z, each drawn up to the point where it fractures. Which material is brittle?

figure.alt: Stress against strain for three materials. X is a steep straight line that ends at a high stress and small strain. Y rises steeply and then flattens over a large strain. Z rises slowly, curving upwards, to a low stress at a very large strain.

questions.solution: A brittle material obeys Hooke's law almost up to the point where it snaps, with little or no plastic deformation: a straight line that ends suddenly, like X. Y has a long, nearly flat plastic region before it fractures, the mark of a ductile material. Z stretches a great deal under a low stress, like a polymer.

questions.q: What is the elastic limit of a material?

options.A: The point beyond which force is no longer proportional to extension.
options.B: The point beyond which the material no longer returns to its original length when unloaded.
options.C: The greatest stress the material can withstand.
options.D: The point at which the material fractures.

questions.solution: Up to the elastic limit a material returns to its original length when the load is removed. Beyond it the deformation is plastic and some extension is permanent. The limit of proportionality, where Hooke's law stops applying, usually comes just before it.

questions.q: What is meant by the breaking stress of a material?

options.A: The stress at which Hooke's law stops applying.
options.B: The force needed to break a sample of the material.
options.C: The stress at which the material fractures.
options.D: The strain at which the material fractures.

questions.solution: Breaking stress is the tensile stress at which the material fractures. It is a stress, so it does not depend on the size of the sample, unlike the breaking force.

questions.q: A metal wire is stretched beyond its elastic limit and then unloaded. The graph shows the force against extension for loading and for unloading. What does the shaded area between the two lines represent?

figure.alt: Force against extension. The loading line rises steeply from the origin and then curves over. The unloading line is straight, parallel to the first part of the loading line, and reaches zero force at a permanent extension. The area between the two lines is shaded.

options.A: The elastic strain energy recovered from the wire.
options.B: The total work done in stretching the wire.
options.C: The Young modulus of the metal.
options.D: The energy that is not recovered, transferred to heating the wire.

questions.solution: The area under the loading line is the total work done; the area under the unloading line is the energy recovered. The area between them is energy used to deform the wire permanently, which ends up heating it.

questions.q: In an experiment to find the Young modulus of a metal, why is a long, thin wire used?

options.A: It gives a larger extension, which reduces the percentage uncertainty in measuring it.
options.B: It makes the Young modulus of the metal larger.
options.C: It stops the wire reaching its elastic limit.
options.D: It reduces the stress in the wire.

questions.solution: For a given load, a longer and thinner wire extends more. A larger extension can be measured with a smaller percentage uncertainty. The Young modulus is a property of the metal and does not depend on the wire's dimensions.

questions.q: Wire X extends by \(e\) under a certain load. Wire Y is made of the same metal but has twice the length and twice the diameter. What is the extension of wire Y under the same load?
questions.solution: From the Young modulus, \(\Delta L = \frac{FL}{AE}\). Twice the length doubles the extension; twice the diameter gives four times the area, which quarters it. Together the extension is half of \(e\).

questions.q: An object of volume \(2.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^{3}\) is fully submerged in water of density \(1000\ \text{kg m}^{-3}\). What is the upthrust on it? (\(g = 9.81\ \text{N kg}^{-1}\))
questions.solution: Upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced: \(U = \rho Vg = 1000 \times 2.0 \times 10^{-4} \times 9.81\) = 2.0 N. Leaving out \(g\) finds the mass of water displaced (0.20 kg), not its weight.

questions.q: Under which conditions does Stokes' law give the viscous drag on an object moving through a fluid?

options.A: Any object moving at any speed.
options.B: A large object moving fast, with turbulent flow.
options.C: A small sphere moving fast, with turbulent flow.
options.D: A small sphere moving slowly, with laminar flow.

questions.solution: Stokes' law, \(F = 6\pi\eta rv\), applies to a small spherical object moving at low speed, where the fluid flows around it in smooth layers (laminar flow). In turbulent flow the drag is much larger.
